items.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: my friend Dan Morgenstern and his friend David Himmelstein, they got to the Little Theater in New York

ctx.x: Yes. Yes. I think so. I think in a sense, and you might say in the early days, the white bands were a bit more polished, but they didn’t swing. You know, that was really, I mean when Basie’s band comes out of Kansas City and there’s a sensation, George Simon, the critic said it was out of tune and everything. And well they were playing with instruments which were battered, had rubber bands and chewing gum on them, that sort of thing. And

of course a lot of those musicians didn’t have the education that white musicians had had. They were probably not good readers to start with. So that was why Basie’s thing stressed head arrangements, which they sort of cooked up themselves. But you know if you take the best black bands of the swing era, from the point of swinging they are undoubtedly very much superior. But you can take Goodman’s band, it’s probably the best of the white bands, Artie Shaw’s, Glenn Miller’s, Tommy Dorsey had a very good band. But…
Well much was made of his innovative work with Louis Armstrong.

items.q: Then I was approached – my old friend Stanley Dance, who had by then settled in the U.S. with his Canadian-born wife Helen Oakley

ctx.x: his position changed drastically, because one of his major clients – I forget what company that was, but they were responsible for about 65% of his business – had presented him with an ultimatum: either he would become their exclusive representative or else they would take their business away from him. He and his partner decided that what they would have to do would be to go along with this. So that changed his position. He was no longer an independent operator. He was a branch of another enterprise. It changed…

This way we were able to introduce a non- – not the usual audience to the artistry on display at the Museum of Modern Art. We had some great moments there. I’ll get back to that later. After Metronome died – we tried. I tried Norman Granz. I thought he was somebody who might be able to buy this magazine. But you know Norman. He didn’t really like jazz writing. That’s one thing that we did share. So he didn’t bite, and the thing went down. We did publish that last issue. Looking back on that, that was the most…

helpful to my career. It was fun to start a magazine, which it really was, starting a magazine, even with Bob as the non-credited actual publisher looking over my shoulder. He was then producing for Impulse!, a label that had been started by Creed Taylor but was very quickly taken over by Bob. Of course he is very famous for his involvement with [John] Coltrane. He was an active producer. He didn’t actually tell me what to do, but there were certain artists that came within our purview, and there were certain…
